footprint.GUIDE:
## Footprint - decide it first (cells of 16 px; a standing person is 1 cell wide, 2 cells tall)
- FOOT rows (bottom) are where the object stands: they block walking. OVER rows above them hold tall parts (awning,
  crown, lamp head, cover); the character walks there and is drawn behind them.
- Usual sizes measured in the target chipsets: crate, barrel, jar, chair, potted plant 1x1; bench, trough, table 2x1;
  bed 1x2 (double 2x2); wardrobe or bookshelf 1x1 + one over row; lamp post 1x1 + two over rows; lone tree 2x1 + two
  over rows (only the trunk row blocks); hand cart 2x1 + 1; wagon 3-4 wide, 1-2 foot rows + 1; market stall 3x2 + 1
  (bigger: 5x2 + 2); fountain 3-4 wide, 2 foot rows + 1; statue 1x1 + 2 (large 2x2 + 2).
- Depth is more FOOT rows; height is more OVER rows. Do not make something tall by stretching its foot.
- The whole picture fits the footprint: width = cells x 16, height = (foot + over) x 16. Nothing pokes past it.

prompts.ANSWER:
## Answer - either A or B
A) ONE JSON object:
{"legend": {"a": "wood:3", "b": "wood:6"}, "rows": ["..aab..", ".abbba.", ...], "note": "what you drew, one line", "topRows": 4,
 "parts": [{"at": [2, 12], "legend": {"o": "glass:0", "m": "glass:3", "h": "glass:5"}, "rows": [".o.", "omo", "omh", "ooo"]}]}
- rows: top to bottom, one character = one pixel, "." = transparent. Row count = canvas height, row length = canvas width.
- parts (optional): drawn over the rows; at = [left x, BOTTOM y]; "." keeps what is under it.
- legend values are palette keys only (`ramp:step`, 0 = darkest).
B) A PNG of exactly the canvas size made by your own draw script (submit with png=PATH): only palette colours, alpha 0 or
   255. Writing a small script with named ramps and part sprites (rows of letters) is the recommended way for anything
   with repeated parts.

DIRECTIONS.A: Chipset-faithful: same outline weight, number of shades and colours as the reference objects, as if it had always been in the chipset.
DIRECTIONS.B: Brief-faithful: every element of the brief, in the most typical SNES-era JRPG shape.
DIRECTIONS.C: Simple and clear: big readable masses at 16px, fewer but larger parts.
DIRECTIONS.D: Ornate: one step richer (pattern, light, material). No dust or noise.
DIRECTIONS.E: Free interpretation: another design for the same use. Keep the canvas.

prompts.JUDGE:
You are an ADVERSARIAL pixel-art judge for a 16px-tile RPG chipset (3/4 top-down view, like RPG Maker / Pokemon).
Your job is to find reasons to REJECT. Default to FAIL when in doubt. You did not draw any of this. Do not run commands,
edit files or trust any claim of success. Look only at the board images.

Open each board image with your Read tool ({n_images} board(s)). Top row of every board = ANCHORS at 6x with a 1x thumbnail:
{anchors}
Bottom row = samples S1..Sn at 6x with a 1x thumbnail, all meant to be "{name}" ({brief}). Some samples were made
deliberately bad to test you and you are not told which; judge every sample on its own.

Judge EACH sample on two axes:
A. view34: a box-like or furniture piece must show a readable lit TOP PLANE (at least ~3 px rows at 1x, visibly a surface
   seen from above, lighter than the front) above its FRONT face. Pure front elevation (top only a 1-2 px line) = FAIL.
   Thin or round objects (posts, stands, models) only need their base/plinth to read as seen from above. Seats (sofas, chairs,
   benches): the SEAT surface must be seen from above (>= ~3 lit rows); backrests and armrests may be
   face-on panels with no top - never FAIL a seat for a face-on backrest or armrest. A bed's headboard is likewise a face-on panel (the mattress top is the plane). Flat floor pieces and wall-hung things are exempt.
   Trees, bushes, plants, rocks and heaps have no top plane: they pass view34 when the top of the mass is lit from above and
   the base sits on the ground line.
B. quality vs the GOOD anchors:
   Q1 silhouette - reads as its name at 1x, parts are separate masses, nothing floats detached.
   Q2 light - >= 3 tones per material, lit from the upper left: tops lightest, fronts mid, undersides darkest; no
      highlights on the shadow side, no random bright blocks or floating "sticker" highlights.
   Q3 outline - in the material's own darkest tone (not pure black boxes around every part), same weight everywhere.
   Q4 proportion, Q5 material texture (grain, seams, a lit metal edge; no big flat fills), Q6 clean (no stray pixels, noise).
   Q7 organic form - for a natural object (tree, bush, plant, flower, food pile, animal, rock): a geometric primitive is a
      FAIL - a crown or bush that is a smooth circle, ellipse, egg or dome (1 px stair steps are not lobes), a crown made
      of round "bubble" clumps each lit on top with a dark crescent under it (cabbage / grapes), a rectangle or straight
      parallel-sided trunk, fruit, flowers or stones that are one stamp (same size, same highlight) or on a grid / even
      scatter, a symmetric silhouette, an even 1 px ring outline, one gradient band instead of fine clustered leaf
      texture, a palette clearly lighter or more pastel than the GOOD anchors, single lightest pixels sprinkled evenly
      over the crown instead of 2-4 px dashes on the lit lobes, a crown or bush that fills a smooth egg/ball envelope
      without deep notches, stones that are rounded-rectangle "pillows" or stacked in rows/courses (2 over 3) like a
      wall, a flower bed seen face-on as a wall strip with one row of same-size blooms, or an object with no dark shadow
      side (the lower right and the gaps as dark as the GOOD anchors' shadows). Compare with the GOOD anchors side by
      side: it must have their asymmetric lobes and notches, fine leaf flecks, dark interior, broken outline, varied
      fruit partly hidden, and a narrow trunk with thin roots.
   FAIL if any of Q1-Q3 or Q7 fails, or two of Q4-Q6, or it is closer to the BAD anchor than to the GOOD ones.
   "It reads as the object" is not a reason to pass.

Output ONLY JSON lines, one per sample, nothing else:
{{"id":"S1","view34":"PASS|FAIL","quality":"PASS|FAIL","reason":"<one short sentence; concrete pixels/parts>"}}

Samples: {ids}
prompts.LARGE:
## Large object - lessons from earlier rounds (docs/lessons.md)
- One footprint, one body. Decide the lit top plane first: the full width, about 25-35% of the height (4-6+ rows);
  depth shows as more top rows. A shallow top makes a heavy object read as another one (a stone coffin read as a
  wardrobe until its top was 12 rows and its front 8).
- Seats, wheels, lamps, signs and contents stay inside the same outline. No separate outlined block under or beside the
  body, no part poking past the footprint, nothing touching the canvas edge; keep a transparent margin.
- Name the 2-3 features that make it recognisable and check them at 1x before any detail.
- Contents go on the wide top plane and vary; no 1-2 px specks of mixed colour, no 1 px checker or speckle, no
  lettering (a sign is a blank panel), no two round blobs side by side (they read as eyes).
- A set (a table with chairs) is one picture: back chairs face-on behind the top, front chairs seen from behind, floor
  visible between the legs.
- Scale against a 24x32 px person: a table top 14-16 px above the floor, a seat 8-10 px, a door 32-40 px tall.
- A 16 px cell border should cut through a plank or a stone, not run along a joint, or the object looks like tiles
  pasted together.
- If the same complaint comes back three times, rebuild the structure (`object-gen underdraw`, or how a passing
  exemplar builds its top) instead of polishing.
prompts.RECIPE:
## How to draw it (what made the good round good)
1. Name the materials first and use their ramps from the palette below (wood, glass, brass, ...). Every pixel is a palette key.
2. Body first: outline, lit top plane (>= 3 rows, lighter than the front, grain = a step up/down in short horizontal
   streaks, lightest front lip row), front face, plinth. Then the parts.
3. Contents are separate PART sprites (bottles, loaves, books, gems ...) placed on their shelf line - vary shape, size
   and position shelf by shelf. Never copy one block across a shelf. Recesses get a shaded back wall (darkest under
   the plank above), not flat black.
4. Light from the upper left, 3-4 tones per material (outline, dark, mid, light), at most ONE 1-px highlight per object,
   on the lit side. No floating "sticker" highlights.
5. Outline = the material's own darkest tone (not pure black), on the shadow sides and the bottom; the row that touches
   the ground is the darkest. Near-black only where the floor would swallow the material's dark. Parts that overlap get
   an inner contour; parts do not each get a box.
6. Keep the canvas, footprint and id. Fix what is broken; do not redraw a good body from a geometric primitive.
prompts.RECIPE_ORGANIC:
## How to draw a natural object (tree, bush, plant, flower, food pile, animal, rock)
Match the hand-drawn exemplars (Beodeul trees and bushes) side by side: they are FOLIAGE TEXTURE, not shapes.
NEVER use a geometric primitive: no circle, ellipse, egg or dome outline for a crown or bush, no rectangle or straight
parallel-sided trunk, no row or grid of identical dots (fruit, flowers, stones), no symmetric silhouette, no filled
rectangle anywhere. Also NOT allowed (an adversarial review rejected exactly this): a crown built from 6-8 round "bubble"
clumps that are each a lit dome with a dark crescent under it (it reads as a cabbage or a bunch of grapes), an even 1 px
outline ring all around, and fruit that is one stamp (same size, same 1 px highlight) repeated.
1. Silhouette, by hand: asymmetric - the crown's widest row and its highest point are off-centre, one shoulder at
   least 3 px higher than the other; never two equal humps or a clover. Bite 1-2 DEEP notches (3+ px into the crown) out of the
   rim and push one lobe out past the rest - a crown that fills a smooth envelope reads as an egg on a stick (CROWNFULL),
   a bush that does reads as a ball or dome (BLOBBY) - even when the brief says "round", round means a rounded HEAP of
   clumps with notches, never a circle. 2-4 big lobes that stick out by 3+ px, 1-2 deep notches (2+ px) between them, the
   left and right sides different, a ragged bottom edge whose leaves hang over the top of the trunk. Small 1 px steps on
   a round outline are not lobes. A few gaps where the background shows through are good. Lobes are broad (4+ px
   thick) - no thin 1-2 px spur or hook sticking out of the crown (it reads as a broken stick), and the underside is
   ragged, never one straight line. A bush or crown is ONE heap: one big main mass with smaller clumps leaning on it.
   Notches bite into a shoulder or a side, never a deep split down the middle - a 2x2 bush drawn as two equal round
   lumps with a V-notch top and bottom was failed by all three reviewers as "twin balls". Fill the canvas: a 2x2 bush
   is about as tall as it is wide (28-32 px), not a low strip.
2. Leaf texture: the crown is packed with small irregular leaf CLUMPS 3-6 px across that overlap at different
   heights - each one a lit 1-3 px top-left, a mid body and a 1-2 px dark pocket at its lower right - like the
   exemplars; never rows of horizontal dashes or stripes (three reviewers called a dash-filled crown "combed, striped,
   from another set"), not smooth fills and not shaded balls. Tone budget for a leafy crown (from the exemplars): about 45% mid green,
   25% lower-mid, 15% dark (the interior behind the front leaves and under each lobe), 5-8% darkest (holes and the
   shadow-side edge), and at most 3% lightest yellow-green as 2-4 px bits (a short dash, an L or a 2x2 nub, varied) on the upper-left of clumps only - never a
   single lightest pixel sprinkled over the crown (that reads as speckle noise; LEAFSPECK fails it). The lower and
   right part of the crown is darker. Use the DARK end of the leaf ramp: the crown must not look lighter or more pastel
   than the exemplars next to it. Take the leaf greens of the chipset's own trees, never the grass keys - a crown in
   lawn green vanishes on the lawn (an apple tree drawn in the grass green failed review for exactly that).
3. Outline: broken. The darkest leaf tone sits only on the lower and right edges and under lobes; along the lit upper-left
   edge the edge pixels are dark or mid green leaves, not an outline. Never one continuous ring.
4. Trunk: narrow and dark (3-5 px wide for a 2-cell tree), slightly tapered, splitting into 1-2 branches that vanish into
   the crown, bark with a lit left edge and dark right edge, and 2-4 thin dark roots spreading 2-4 px along the ground
   row, attached to the trunk (no loose blocks).
5. Fruit, flowers, berries, stones are SHADED little bodies, never flat one-colour blocks (a flat pure-red 2x2 block
   reads as a sticker - the last reviews failed exactly that). Use 3 tones of the fruit ramp plus a pale red/pink key
   for a highlight - never near-white (nothing in the exemplars is that bright; a white fleck pops like a sticker).
   Hang the fruit in 2-4 small groups in the lower and outer foliage, not spread evenly round the rim. Apple sprites in letters (h highlight, r mid red, d dark red, k darkest red, g leaf):
     3x3 lit "hr." / "rrd" / ".dk"   2x2 lit "hr" / "rd"   2x2 in shade "dd" / "dk"   half hidden "gr" / "gd"
     1x2 peeking "r" / "d"   pair ".hr" / "hrd" / "rdk"
   About half the fruit is in shade (d/k only) or partly covered by leaf pixels; only 2-3 get the h pixel.
   No two the same. Mix sizes (1x1, 2x1, 2x2, 3x2), give at most half of them a 1 px
   highlight, draw 2-3 in shade with the darker red, cover 2-3 partly with leaf pixels, cluster some in twos, leave
   irregular gaps. Never the same shape on a grid or an even scatter.
6. Flower beds and planters: the plants are the object. A loose, mounded mass of leaves that spills over an uneven low
   edge (stones of different sizes and shapes, some hidden by leaves - or no edge at all), never a rectangular box of
   equal blocks. Flowers grow in drifts of one colour (3-6 blooms together), each bloom a different small cluster of a
   lit petal, a shaded petal and maybe a centre - sizes 1x1 to 3x2, some half hidden by leaves. Never a plus/cross
   stamp, never one flower per cell on a grid. Bloom shapes in letters (P lit petal, p shaded petal, c centre, g leaf):
     "Pp" / "pc"    "Ppp" / "gpc"    "P"    "pP." / ".cp"    "gP" / "pp"
   In 3/4 view the bed is seen from above: its top (soil and plants, flowers scattered over the whole top at different
   depths, back ones smaller and higher) takes most of the height; the front rim or soil edge is only 2-4 px tall, never
   a face-on wall strip, and the flowers never stand in one row along the front.
   An adversarial review failed exactly this: a stone box of same-size blocks with repeated red/yellow/white crosses, and
   then a face-on stone strip with one row of same-size blooms on top.
7. Food piles, heaps and rocks: a slumped, asymmetric pile - wide at the base, an irregular top - of lumps of clearly
   different sizes: one big anchor lump and smaller ones leaning on or tucked against it, overlapping, never laid in
   rows or courses like a wall. Stones are ANGULAR: flat facets, chipped corners, a concave notch - never pillows or
   rounded rectangles: every stone has at least one hard corner, one flat broken face and a notch, and one stone is
   tilted or overhangs so the pile's outline is not a smooth mound. No rows: stones overlap at different heights and
   angles (never two on top of a row of three). Give the pile a dark shadow side (lower right) and a darker contact
   edge on the ground, as dark as the exemplar trees' shadow side; the lit upper left may run straight into the grass. Light each lump on its own upper-left facet with a
   clustered highlight (not top-to-bottom bands), and fill the gaps between lumps with NEAR-BLACK pockets from the
   darkest keys - as dark as the exemplar trees' shadows, about a tenth of the pile (NODEEP fails less than 8%) - with
   cracks across the big ones. Moss sits in clumped caps on the upper lit faces and
   spills into a few gaps - not as even mortar lines between every stone. Animals: a living body with a head, legs and a
   tail from the side or 3/4 - no boxes.
8. Look at 1x next to the exemplars: if the crown reads as a coin, an egg, a lollipop, a cabbage or a bunch of grapes, or
   is lighter than the exemplars, break the silhouette and redraw the texture.
9. Build the crown from MANY SMALL clusters (2-5 px), not a few big lobes: never stack 4-6 big lobes in tiers that
   each get a light cap stroke, a flat mid-green body and a dark crescent under it (two reviewers called that "cloud
   shelves" / cabbage). Scatter small DARK HOLES (1-3 px of the two darkest keys) all through the crown interior -
   about 3 per 100 leaf pixels, as in the exemplars (LEAFHOLES fails fewer than 2.2) - and short light dashes across the
   whole upper-left half, not one per lobe top. Light and dark change every few pixels, at every height.
10. Leaf texture is CLUMPS, not dither and not stripes: in the exemplar most pixels sit in small same-tone patches of
   2-6 px running in different directions (horizontal, diagonal, little blobs); single isolated pixels are rare, and no
   two neighbouring rows repeat the same dash pattern. Random 1 px speckle reads as noise, smooth fills read as plastic,
   stacked parallel dashes read as stripes.
11. No straight walls: the crown's left and right sides bulge in and out lobe by lobe - the edge x changes every 1-3
   rows in the exemplars. A side that runs straight down 6+ rows reads as a box (three reviewers failed a crown with a
   16 px straight left wall; STRAIGHTSIDE fails more than 10). The widest row sits in the middle or lower half of the
   crown and overhangs the trunk.

Beodeul broadleaf tree B (an exemplar, 47x56 px) in letters - 0 darkest .. 5 lightest leaf green, a-d bark dark to light,
"." transparent. Study the density, not the shape: the upper-left edge is light leaves (4/5) with NO outline, the
darkest 0/1 only along the lower right and under the crown, 2-6 px runs of one tone, dark pockets (0/1/2) inside,
a few 5 dashes (never single 5 pixels) on top of lobes, ragged lobed outline, the trunk 5-7 px with bark tones and roots on the ground row.
Do not copy it whole. DO build your leaf texture from its patches: cut 4-8 px pieces of these rows (a clump with its
light dash and the dark pocket under it, a ragged edge piece) and rearrange and overlap them inside your own
silhouette, at your own canvas size. Digit n = the n-th key of the "Leaf greens" list below (0 darkest .. 5 lightest),

prompts.VIEW:
## View - the chipset's 3/4 top-down view
- The camera is south of the object looking down. A standing object shows its TOP surfaces seen from above (foreshortened)
  AND its FRONT (south) face. A pure front elevation (the top only a 1-2 px line) is wrong. A pure plan view is wrong.
- Every horizontal surface - top, lid, seat, shelf plank, table top, roof, column cap, the inside of an open container -
  is visible from above: >= 3 rows for furniture, lighter than the front face, with the lightest row at its front lip.
- Depth (north-south) shows as the number of rows of the top plane, never as a taller front. Something long north-south
  is long on screen because its top is long.
- Seats: the SEAT surface is seen from above; a backrest or armrests may be drawn face-on.
- An object that faces east or west shows its own side profile as its south face; that is normal.
- The lowest painted row is the ground line (canvas bottom). Do not paint floor, shadows on the floor or background.
- Unsure about a round or deep shape? `object-gen underdraw` renders boxes, cylinders, tunnels and spheres in this view
  at 1x (top = yellow, front = blue). Draw over it.
prompts.VIEW_ORGANIC:
## View - the chipset's 3/4 top-down view, for a natural object
- The camera is south of it looking down: the top of a crown, bush, heap or rock is seen from above and catches the light
  (upper left), its south side is in shade. There is no flat top plane to draw - the lit top is the upper part of the mass.
- The lowest painted row is the ground line: roots, the base of the bush or the bottom stones sit on it. Do not paint the
  floor, a shadow on the floor or a background.
- Do not start from `object-gen underdraw` spheres or cylinders: those are for furniture. Build the mass by hand.

reference.NEGATIVE: straight-on front elevation, eye-level camera, camera at or below the top surface, isometric view, diagonal view, rotated object, visible side face, perspective lines vanishing to the side, worm's-eye view, close-up crop, product photo angle
reference.NEGATIVE_LOW: a top-dominant view where the top fills most of the picture, a high bird's-eye view, a plan view from directly above, a straight-on front elevation with no top surface visible, isometric view, diagonal view, rotated object, visible side face, perspective lines vanishing to the side, close-up crop
reference.SIZE_NOTE: Size: on the map it covers {w} by {h} cells (width by height); a standing person is 1 cell wide and 2 cells tall - keep that size relative to a person and that width-to-height proportion ({w}:{h}).
reference.STYLE_NOTE: The attached image shows finished objects of the target game drawn in exactly this camera angle (top plane large, short front, no side faces). Match that CAMERA ANGLE and level of simplification only; draw the new object described here, do not copy the objects in the attached image.
reference.STYLE_NOTE_LOW: The attached image shows finished objects of the target game in exactly this proportion (top band about a third of the height, tall front). Match that camera angle and proportion only; draw the new object described here, do not copy the objects in the attached image.

The TOP surface ({top}) is clearly visible as a large flat plane that takes up most of the object's height in the picture; the front face is short and sits directly below it. Left and right edges stay vertical and parallel; no side face is visible. Clean simple game-asset illustration, simple shapes, soft light from the upper left, plain flat light-grey background, no floor, no room, no text, no people, the whole object in frame and centered. Object: {d}
reference.VIEW_LOW: Classic 16-bit RPG town-map view, gentle top-down 3/4 view: the camera is LOW, about 30 to 35 degrees above the horizontal, looking north at the object from the south. It is not a high bird's-eye view. The TOP surface ({top}) shows as a band across the top of the object: about {target} percent of the object's visible height (between {lo} and {hi} percent). The front face below it is the main mass, about {rest} percent of the height, with its details large and clearly visible. Left and right edges stay vertical and parallel; no side face is visible. Clean simple game-asset illustration, simple shapes, soft light from the upper left, plain flat light-grey background, no ground, no text, no people, the whole object in frame and centered. Object: {d}
reference.VIEW_PROMPT:
You check ONE reference picture for a pixel-art game. It must show the object in the 3/4 top-down RPG
view: camera high above at about 60 degrees looking down from the south, the TOP surface visible as a large plane, a short
front face below it, no side faces, vertical left/right edges. Reject anything else, be strict:
- "front": straight-on front elevation or eye level - the top is a thin sliver or invisible
- "isometric": diagonal/rotated object, two faces visible, edges not vertical
- "side": a side face visible, or perspective vanishing to one side
- "low": camera at or below the top surface
- "other": not one object, cropped, a room, text
Answer with ONE line of JSON only: {"view": "top34|front|isometric|side|low|other", "topShare": <percent of the object's
picture height that is top surface>, "why": "<one short sentence>"}
reference.VIEW_PROMPT_LOW:
You check ONE reference picture for a pixel-art game. It must show the object in the LOW 3/4 town-map
view: camera about 30-35 degrees above the horizontal, looking north from the south; the TOP surface (for a building, the
roof) shows as a band across the top, and the front face below it is the main mass. No side faces, vertical left/right
edges. Measure topShare yourself: the top surface's height (from its highest point down to the front edge or eave) as a
percent of the object's whole visible height in the picture. Classify:
- "top34low": that low 3/4 view - a visible top band plus a tall front, no side face, edges vertical
- "top34": a high 3/4 view where the top is the largest plane
- "front": straight-on front elevation - no top surface visible, or only a sliver under 10 percent
- "isometric": diagonal/rotated object, two faces visible, edges not vertical
- "side": a side face visible, or perspective vanishing to one side
- "low": camera below the top surface (looking up)
- "other": not one object, cropped, a scene, text
Answer with ONE line of JSON only: {"view": "top34low|top34|front|isometric|side|low|other", "topShare": <percent>,
"why": "<one short sentence>"}
